Grooved mullet (Chelon dumerili) exhibits life-history traits broadly similar to those of other mugilids, though species-specific data remain sparse. Field-collected adults from coastal lagoon systems in the eastern Mediterranean yield a maximum recorded total length for females of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper range documented for congeneric species of comparable ecological habit. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of mature individuals, reaches 794 grams [Wwi = 794 grams], indicating a moderately robust body form typical of benthic-feeding mugilids. This mass is attained gradually over several years of somatic growth, with the fastest increases in weight observed during the second and third years of life. Sexual maturation is linked to size rather than age in this species, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. The wet weight at puberty, calculated from the same length-weight relationship, is 34.4 grams [Wwp = 34.4 grams], a relatively modest size that allows the onset of reproductive activity early in the life cycle.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females peaked at approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] at a water temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C]. The timing of the annual reproductive cycle in Chelon dumerili is closely tied to thermal cues; rising spring temperatures stimulate vitellogenesis, while the peak spawning period coincides with the warmest months of the year. Field surveys from the Gulf of Gabès indicate that gravid females are most frequently encountered between June and August, when surface water temperatures routinely exceed 25 °C. The relationship between temperature and gonadal development likely reflects an evolutionary adaptation to the predictable seasonal warming of shallow coastal habitats that promote high larval survival and rapid early growth.

The initial stages of embryonic development in Grooved mullet are characterized by a very small egg size, with the freshly fertilized, water-hardened ovum having a diameter of approximately 0.9 millimeters. Based on this egg diameter, the calculated ultimate wet weight per individual egg is 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], an extremely modest mass that reflects the high fecundity typical of pelagic-spawning mugilids. Eggs are released into the water column during mass spawning events that involve multiple males pursuing a single female, a behaviour that maximizes fertilization success. The small, transparent, and buoyant eggs drift with the currents during the 48- to 72-hour incubation period, after which the yolk-sac larvae emerge at a length of about 2.5 millimeters. These early-stage larvae are entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves for their first few days of life. The onset of exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and the first successful capture of rotifers or small copepod nauplii, typically occurs between the fourth and sixth day post-hatching, depending on water temperature and prey availability.

Longevity records for Chelon dumerili come primarily from tag-recapture studies conducted in coastal lagoons of the northern Adriatic Sea, where individuals are known to persist for a maximum lifespan of approximately 3,650 days [am = approximately 3,650 days] under the thermal regime characteristic of that region, which averages 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] during the active growing season. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly a decade, is moderate for a mugilid of this body size; related species such as Chelon labrosus have been reported to live slightly longer, while the smaller Liza ramada exhibits a shorter maximum longevity. The age structure of wild populations is typically dominated by individuals between two and six years old, with older fish becoming progressively rarer due to natural mortality and fishing pressure. Growth in length slows markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, a pattern that is common among iteroparous teleosts that continue to allocate energy to reproduction throughout their adult lives. Annual growth increments in fish older than eight years are often less than 1 centimeter per year.

The reproductive strategy of Grooved mullet involves a single protracted spawning season each year, during which individual females release multiple batches of eggs. Data from captive broodstock maintained at the 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] thermal regime show that females produce approximately 1.2 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1.2 million eggs per spawning event], with a typical frequency of 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = 1 spawning event per year]. This high fecundity compensates for the extremely small egg mass and the substantial mortality experienced during the early planktonic stages. The onset of first reproduction in the wild is tied to the attainment of a threshold body size rather than a fixed chronological age, but available data suggest that females typically participate in their first spawning at an age of approximately 2 years. The combination of early maturation, high fecundity, and batch spawning allows Chelon dumerili to maintain stable populations despite moderate fishing pressure. Comparative studies with other mugilids indicate that this reproductive output is intermediate between the relatively low fecundity of the freshwater-adapted Myxus capensis and the extremely high fecundity of the catadromous Mugil cephalus.
